newsitem.title: CROATIA: European entry boosts fragile democracy in Croatia.
newsitem.headline: European entry boosts fragile democracy in Croatia.

text.p: The Council of Europe's decision on Wednesday to admit Croatia despite concerns about its human rights record aims to spur the ex-Yugoslav republic into embracing democracy, diplomats said.
The long delayed announcement by the Council, seen as an antechamber to the European Union, makes Croatia the second ex-Yugoslav republic after Slovenia to knock on the door of Western integration.
Croatia will be formally inducted into the organisation, which binds members to European covenants on democracy and human rights, in a ceremony on November 6.
Six months after shelving Croatia's application over human rights issues, the Strasbourg-based Council said Zagreb had now made sufficient amends to be admitted.

The Council verdict was welcome news for Croatia's nationalist government whose poll ratings have been declining over alleged corruption and a war-induced impoverishment of the middle class ahead of major elections next year.

European diplomats in Zagreb said the decision credited Croatia for progress made under Western prodding in the past six months. But considerably more remained to be achieved on a long and winding road to integration in the EU and NATO.
"This is not a seal of approval for the status quo in Croatia, which is still halfway between a war situation and a democratic society," said one senior diplomat.

"But a consensus was reached in the Council that it would be more constructive to admit Croatia, introducing an institutional impetus or pressure on Croatia to embrace democracy, than rejecting it yet again."
Prime Minister Zlatko Matesa said: "Croatia has now shown it respects and complies with its international commitments."
Foreign Minister Mate Granic said Croatia would now focus on joining central European integration schemes as well as NATO's Partnership for Peace programme.
Croatia hurdled barriers to Council membership recently by forging diplomatic relations with Serbia, its arch-enemy in the nationalist wars over Yugoslavia's breakup in 1991-95.
It also ensured Bosnian Croats cooperated with post-war unity elections in Bosnia, widened a war amnesty for minority Serbs in Croatia and enacted a bill defining media freedoms.
But European diplomats said Croatia still lagged on several crucial aspects of democratic behaviour and the rule of law.

They cited its failure to extradite Croats indicted by the U.N. tribunal on war crimes in former Yugoslavia, accept an opposition victory in Zagreb municipal elections and resettle Serb war refugees with guarantees of equal rights.

Doubts also lingered about right-wing intolerance towards free media -- the government has appealed against the acquittal of two journalists charged with insulting President Franjo Tudjman -- and Zagreb's intentions towards the Serb minority.
A litmus test will be the fate of 120,000 Serbs in the last separatist enclave of Croatia which is to be "reintegrated" in Croatia under U.N. supervision by mid-1997.

"We will probably have to see advances on all these issues before Croatia moves closer to the EU club, with a trade and cooperation agreement, then an association agreement, and so on," said another European diplomat.

In joining the Council, Croatia pledged to ratify the European Convention on Human Rights within a year and recognise the ultimate jurisdiction of the European Court of Human Rights, to which Croat citizens may now seek legal recourse.
The government has also formed a parliamentary committee to bring all its laws into line with European standards.
Croatia's constitution is broadly democratic but state-manipulated courts and police have often failed to enforce it, especially in areas of minority rights and press freedoms, diplomats say.
